RVV is a general vector substrate; Tensor Cores are specialized matrix units. The RISC-V Matrix Extension (AME/IME) would be the direct competitor if ratified.
GPU architecture provides contrast for VLA vs. SIMT vs. fixed-width SIMD design philosophy.

ISA proposals (AME/IME/VME) decompose into specific multi-PE microarchitectural organizations — the ISA defines what instructions exist, the microarchitecture defines how PEs execute them spatially.
All multi-PE matrix microarchitectures except pure systolic arrays depend on RVV for vector operand supply and non-GEMM kernel execution.
The choice of multi-PE organization (clustered vs. systolic vs. accumulator-extended) constrains which kernel mapping strategies achieve high utilization.

RISC-V multi-PE matrix organizations are an architecturally distinct alternative to NVIDIA Tensor Cores for matrix acceleration — both spatially parallelize matrix multiply across hardware PEs but differ in ISA integration (CPU ISA extension vs. GPU warp-level primitive).

Multi-PE matrix microarchitectures use explicit spatial PE organization (systolic arrays, clustered VPUs) as an alternative execution model to SIMT warp-level thread parallelism. The PE is a hardware concept; the thread is a software concept.

The multi-PE memory hierarchy (shared L1 scratchpad in Spatz, weight-stationary buffers in Quadrilatero) inherits design principles from GPU memory hierarchies — both must manage data supply to parallel compute units.

RISC-V vector memory hierarchy design decisions (scratchpad vs. cache, burst access modes) directly enable or constrain multi-PE matrix scaling, as demonstrated by MemPool-Spatz TCDM burst access enabling 1024-FPU clusters.
Multi-PE microarchitecture decomposes into interconnect fabric design — the PE organization determines the communication pattern the NoC must support.
NoC design for matrix accelerators depends on memory hierarchy decisions — scratchpad banking, DMA engine placement, and burst access modes directly constrain interconnect topology choice.
Interconnect topology choice is constrained by scale-up vs. scale-out strategy — shared-L1 suits scale-up within a cluster, mesh NoC suits scale-out across clusters.
Memory hierarchy design enables interconnect scaling — TCDM burst access in MemPool-Spatz enables 1024-FPU shared-L1 clusters without interconnect saturation.
RISC-V NoC-based PE interconnect (shared L1, mesh NoC) competes architecturally with GPU shared memory + crossbar interconnect as data supply models for parallel compute units.
Matrix ISA proposals (AME/IME/VME) decompose into a software enablement problem — each ISA requires compiler, library, and framework integration to be useful.
The AI software ecosystem depends on compiler auto-vectorization quality — without good baseline RVV code generation, framework-level optimizations start from a weak foundation.
The software stack depends on efficient kernel patterns (GEMM, attention, convolution) — libraries and compilers target these patterns as their optimization primitives.
The AI software ecosystem inherits the DSL-compiler-runtime separation — ML frameworks occupy the DSL layer, MLIR/TVM the compiler layer, and LiteRT/ONNX Runtime the execution layer.
Software stack performance depends on the underlying NoC/interconnect — the compiler must be aware of communication topology to generate efficient multi-PE code.
Multi-PE microarchitectural design choices are characterized and compared using roofline analysis — the roofline reveals whether a given design is compute-bound or memory-bound.
RISC-V-specific roofline modeling depends on the general roofline theory — compute roof, bandwidth roof, and arithmetic intensity are universal concepts applied to RISC-V hardware parameters.
AI kernel mapping efficiency on RVV is measured by roofline analysis — the gap between achieved and peak FLOP/s reveals optimization headroom.
The bandwidth roof in a RISC-V roofline model depends directly on the vector memory hierarchy design — scratchpad size, banking, and burst modes determine peak bandwidth.
The roofline model is constrained by NoC/interconnect bandwidth — for multi-cluster systems, inter-cluster link bandwidth becomes the limiting roof for distributed GEMM.
The AI software ecosystem decomposes into a runtime execution layer — compilers and libraries produce code, but the runtime decides when and where it executes on multi-PE hardware.
Runtime dispatch performance depends directly on NoC latency and bandwidth — the scheduler must account for inter-PE communication cost when assigning tiles.
Runtime memory management depends on the vector memory hierarchy — scratchpad banking, DMA engine capabilities, and burst access modes constrain allocation strategies.
Runtime dispatch granularity is constrained by PE microarchitecture — the minimum schedulable unit is determined by PE count and per-PE tile size.
Single-chip multi-PE microarchitecture decomposes into the multi-chip scale-out problem — the PE is the building block, and the cluster is the scaled system.
Distributed RISC-V AI clusters are a concrete instantiation of the scale-out strategy — the general scale-up vs. scale-out framework provides the analytical lens.
Inter-node network performance in distributed clusters depends on the intra-chip NoC design — the same bandwidth/latency/area trade-offs recur at larger scale.
Distributed runtime execution (multi-node scheduling, gradient synchronization) builds on single-node multi-PE runtime primitives.
Distributed RISC-V cluster technology decomposes into a supply-chain and business question — who builds these clusters, at what cost, and under what competitive dynamics?
The business case for RISC-V explains the market logic behind scale-out strategies — low per-node cost makes scale-out economically rational.
Multi-PE microarchitecture decomposes into its circuit-level foundation — the SRAM arrays and CIM macros that supply operands to PEs.
SRAM circuit design enables the memory hierarchy — the bitcell topology, banking strategy, and memory compiler capabilities determine achievable bandwidth and capacity at each hierarchy level.
Circuit-level SRAM design decomposes into the manufacturing question — how are these circuits fabricated, packaged, and integrated into working AI accelerators?
Advanced packaging enables scale-up — 2.5D/3D integration is the physical realization of making one local domain larger, tighter, and faster.
Manufacturing and packaging technologies exist to mitigate fundamental physical limits — the physics determines what manufacturing must overcome.
The roofline model's ceilings (compute roof, bandwidth roof) are ultimately constrained by physical limits — thermal, power, and wire delay.
Supply chain business dynamics decompose into the market narrative — the story investors tell about why RISC-V will win, which drives the capital that funds the supply chain.
The market narrative explains the investment logic for distributed RISC-V AI clusters — cost-efficient scale-out is the economic story that attracts hyperscaler capital.

RVV 1.0 compute substrate decomposes into execution architecture — the ISA defines what instructions exist; the execution architecture defines how they are pipelined, issued, and coordinated across PEs.

RISC-V execution models (in-order vector, OoO vector, many-core spatial) are architecturally distinct alternatives to GPU SIMT/warp execution. Where SIMT uses hardware-managed threads to hide latency, RISC-V uses software-managed vectors or explicit PE coordination. Each has different area/throughput tradeoffs.

RISC-V execution architecture spans a spectrum from in-order narrow vector to OoO wide vector to many-core spatial — competing with the GPU execution model (SM + warp scheduler) at every point. The key structural difference: RISC-V lacks hardware warp scheduling, trading utilization on irregular workloads for area efficiency on regular AI kernels.

Execution architecture (pipeline depth, issue width, OoO vs in-order, coordination mechanism) enables or constrains multi-PE microarchitectural choices. The PE is a spatial concept; the execution architecture determines how efficiently each PE can be utilized.

The runtime dispatch model is constrained by the execution architecture — in-order PEs require static scheduling (MultiVic pattern), while OoO PEs can tolerate dynamic dispatch. The coordination mechanism (barriers, queues, dataflow triggers) is determined by what the execution architecture provides in hardware.

RISC-V execution architecture is a concept within the AI accelerator ontology — the execution model is one dimension of accelerator classification alongside compute substrate, memory hierarchy, and programming interface.

SRAM/CIM is the memory circuit foundation; digital IP blocks (DMA, NoC, memory controllers, compute units) are the logic circuit foundation of AI SoCs. Both are circuit-IP-primitives that must be co-designed for area, power, and bandwidth.

The multi-PE microarchitecture is physically realized by assembling digital IP blocks — DMA engines move data, NoC routers connect PEs, memory controllers feed scratchpads. The quality of these IP blocks directly constrains PE utilization and scalability.

The vector memory hierarchy (scratchpad banking, burst access, DMA staging) depends on memory controller and DMA IP quality. High-bandwidth multi-bank scratchpads require memory controllers that can schedule concurrent accesses without bank conflicts.

NoC router IP is the circuit-level realization of interconnect topology. FlooNoC demonstrates that domain-specific NoC IP (wide links, multistream DMA, dedicated control paths) achieves 3× energy efficiency over general-purpose NoCs.

RISC-V AI SoC IP blocks (DMA + NoC + memory controller) compete architecturally with GPU integrated memory hierarchy IP (crossbar + L2 cache controller + HBM PHY) — both are digital IP assemblies, but optimized for different execution models (software-managed vs. hardware-managed memory).
Chiplet-ready IP (UCIe D2D, AMBA CHI C2C) depends on advanced packaging for physical realization. The IP defines the protocol; the packaging defines the physical channel.

Advanced packaging is the back-end assembly process; process node selection and wafer fabrication is the front-end manufacturing process. Both are manufacturing-process-integration concerns that co-determine AI accelerator cost, yield, and performance.
Process node economics are ultimately bounded by physical limits — transistor scaling limits, power density, and SRAM bitcell stability determine what a node can achieve and at what cost.

SRAM/CIM circuit design depends on process node characteristics — SRAM bitcell density, leakage, and variability are determined by the fabrication process. The SRAM scaling gap at advanced nodes directly impacts CIM viability.

Digital IP block design is constrained by the process node — IP must be qualified for a specific node, and porting IP across nodes is a major cost. The reticle limit constrains maximum die area for any single IP block.
Scale-up vs. scale-out strategy is constrained by fabrication economics — the reticle limit bounds monolithic scale-up, while chiplet-based scale-up depends on advanced packaging yield and cost.

GPU architecture design is constrained by process node economics — NVIDIA's ~800 mm² dies push against the reticle limit, and each node transition requires multi-billion-dollar design investments. The GPU market structure is partly a consequence of wafer fabrication economics.

NoC topology design decomposes into power and thermal modeling — the chosen topology determines per-hop energy, total interconnect power, and hotspot distribution. These physical constraints feed back into topology selection.

Memory hierarchy energy costs (scratchpad access, DMA transfer, DRAM access) are the dominant component of total data movement energy. The interconnect power model quantifies why deeper hierarchies exist: to keep data at lower energy tiers for more operations.
Interconnect power is ultimately bounded by physical limits — wire delay, parasitic capacitance, and thermal resistance determine the minimum energy per bit-meter and maximum heat flux.

Thermal management for 2.5D/3D AI accelerators depends on advanced packaging — diamond heat spreaders, microfluidic channels, and TIM materials are packaging-level solutions to interconnect power density.

The roofline model's bandwidth ceiling is, at the physical level, determined by interconnect power and thermal limits. The maximum sustainable bandwidth is set by the power and thermal budget available to the NoC and memory interfaces.

Process node selection determines interconnect energy efficiency — wire capacitance, metal layer count, and transistor drive strength are node-dependent. Advanced nodes improve logic energy but wire energy scales more slowly.

General physical limits (Dennard scaling, power density) decompose into the fundamental energy limit of computation (Landauer) and the beyond-CMOS technologies that may circumvent current scaling limits.

Interconnect power models are ultimately bounded by the Landauer limit and wire delay physics. The 10⁶-10⁷× gap between CMOS interconnect energy and the thermodynamic floor defines the optimization headroom.

SRAM and CIM circuit efficiency is bounded by fundamental switching energy limits. STT-MTJ (spintronic) and other beyond-CMOS memory technologies may eventually replace SRAM for certain AI memory tiers.

Process node roadmap is ultimately determined by physical limits. The end of CMOS scaling (~0.5nm equivalent, ~2030-2035) will force the transition to beyond-CMOS technologies for continued density improvement.

The roofline model's compute and bandwidth ceilings have a thermodynamic floor that cannot be crossed. Reversible computing raises the effective ceiling by reducing the energy cost per useful FLOP, but the per-bit-erasure floor remains.

Auto-vectorization quality is the baseline compiler capability; ML compiler lowering (MLIR/TVM/IREE) is the structured, multi-level approach that achieves higher utilization through domain-specific optimizations like VLEN-aware tiling and microkernel libraries.
ML compilers depend on the broader AI software ecosystem for frontend integration (PyTorch/ONNX), runtime execution (IREE runtime, TVM runtime), and kernel libraries (SKL, OpenBLAS).
Compiler tiling and microkernel generation depend on known-good kernel mapping patterns (GEMM tiling, conv im2col, attention flash). The compiler encodes these patterns as lowering rules.

VLEN-aware tiling is directly constrained by the RVV ISA — VLEN, LMUL, SEW, and register count determine valid tile dimensions. The compiler lowering must be parameterized by these hardware parameters.
Compiler lowering produces the code that the runtime dispatchs. IREE's bytecode and TVM's graph executor are the runtime targets that the compiler generates for.

RISC-V investment narrative is a sub-story within the broader AI semiconductor competitive landscape. RISC-V's market opportunity depends on the dynamics (NVIDIA monopoly, inference fragmentation, foundry gatekeeper) described at the industry level.

The competitive landscape explains why RISC-V supply chain dynamics matter — the NVIDIA monopoly creates demand for alternatives, the HBM bottleneck constrains all players equally, and TSMC gatekeeping affects RISC-V startups disproportionately.
Foundry concentration (TSMC ~90%) explains the economic logic of process node selection — customers don't choose nodes freely; they take what TSMC allocates.

NVIDIA's market dominance is explained by the CUDA platform moat, not just GPU hardware superiority. The GPU architecture overview describes the hardware; the competitive landscape explains why that hardware commands 80%+ market share.

The market structure (NVIDIA monopoly training, fragmented inference, custom ASIC growth) explains why scale-out strategies matter — inference at scale favors many smaller chips, and the desire to reduce NVIDIA dependency drives custom scale-out architectures.
Roofline models the performance ceiling; TCO models the economic cost of approaching that ceiling. Together they form the complete performance-cost-utilization picture.
TCO is dominated by power and cooling costs. Interconnect power efficiency and thermal design directly determine the OpEx component of TCO.
Wafer and packaging costs are the largest single Capex component. Process node choice determines chip cost, which drives the amortized hardware cost per token.
GPU pricing (the largest Capex line item) is determined by market structure. NVIDIA's monopoly pricing power directly inflates TCO for AI infrastructure buyers.

RISC-V distributed clusters have a TCO-driven market logic: lower per-chip cost enables profitable deployment at utilization levels where GPU on-prem would be uneconomical. The RISC-V TCO window is moderate-scale inference at 30-50% utilization.

The roofline model provides the performance ceiling; TCO translates that ceiling into economic terms. A design at 90% of roofline may have worse TCO than one at 70% if the additional 20% costs 3× more.

RISC-V distributed cluster hardware decomposes into the inference serving software layer — disaggregated prefill/decode, KV-cache routing, and scheduling that make the hardware useful for production AI workloads.
Distributed serving depends on per-node runtime execution — the scheduler dispatches work to individual runtime instances that manage PE allocation and memory on each node.

Disaggregated serving enables better TCO by independently scaling prefill and decode hardware, improving utilization of each tier. Without disaggregation, monolithic clusters waste GPUs on whichever phase is underutilized.
The serving scheduler's routing decisions (prefill vs. decode) depend on kernel-level performance characteristics — GEMM kernels for prefill, attention kernels for decode, element-wise for both.

Disaggregated serving maps naturally to heterogeneous PE configurations — wide matrix PEs for prefill, many small vector PEs for decode. The microarchitecture determines which serving phase each PE is best suited for.

Kernel-level mapping (GEMM, attention, element-wise) decomposes into the serving-level mapping problem — how to schedule heterogeneous requests across heterogeneous hardware using those kernels as building blocks.
Multi-model serving depends on the distributed serving infrastructure — disaggregated prefill/decode and KV-cache routing provide the infrastructure that multi-model schedulers optimize over.
Batching and scheduling decisions are constrained by per-node runtime capabilities — maximum batch size, KV-cache capacity, and dispatch latency determine feasible scheduling granularity.
Intelligent batching and multi-model routing improve GPU utilization, directly reducing TCO per token. The 3.58× throughput from bucket-based batching translates to ~3× lower cost per token.

Multi-model serving maps naturally to heterogeneous PE configurations — small PEs for tiny models, wide matrix PEs for base model prefill, many PEs for base model decode. The microarchitecture determines which model variants each PE type can serve efficiently.
RISC-V AI supply chain decomposes into the inference-as-a-service business model layer — how RISC-V hardware reaches the market through neoclouds, token factories, and GPU marketplaces.

The inference economy (token pricing, neocloud fragmentation) explains the market logic for multi-model serving — the long tail of fine-tuned models needs infrastructure that GPU-hour pricing can't economically serve.
Inference-as-a-service unit economics depend on TCO models — the token price must exceed the amortized hardware + opex cost per token, or the business is unsustainable.

Inference business models are shaped by the semiconductor competitive landscape — NVIDIA's hardware monopoly enables the token factory model, while GPU commoditization would favor capital-light aggregation.

The inference economy explains why disaggregated serving matters — if prefill and decode have different economics (compute-bound vs memory-bound), serving them from the same GPU is economically suboptimal.
Single-tenant PE dispatch decomposes into the multi-tenant scheduling problem — priority classes, QoS guarantees, preemption, and interference isolation across tenants sharing the same hardware.
Multi-tenant scheduling enables multi-model serving — without QoS guarantees, serving heterogeneous models on shared GPUs creates priority inversion that violates SLOs.
Multi-tenant QoS is the technical foundation for inference-as-a-service business models — token factories need guaranteed SLOs to sell differentiated service tiers.

Scheduling granularity is constrained by the execution architecture — GPU preemption at batch boundaries (20-50ms) vs. RISC-V PE preemption at tile boundaries (µs). The execution architecture determines the minimum schedulable unit.
Multi-tenant scheduling at node level feeds into distributed serving — the cluster scheduler routes requests to nodes based on per-node QoS state.

AI software ecosystem decomposes into declarative QoS specification — the programming interface that lets applications express latency/throughput/priority requirements without hard-coding scheduling logic.
Declarative QoS is the specification layer; multi-tenant scheduling is the implementation layer. SLO-as-code drives scheduler decisions.
Declarative QoS enables differentiated inference service tiers — the technical foundation for token-based pricing with guaranteed SLOs.
Declarative QoS specification depends on the DSL/compiler/runtime separation — the specification is the DSL; the SLA Planner is the compiler; the scheduler is the runtime.

Declarative QoS is the specification layer; multi-tenant scheduling is the implementation layer. SLO-as-code drives scheduler decisions.

Declarative QoS specification depends on the DSL/compiler/runtime separation — the specification is the DSL; the SLA Planner is the compiler; the scheduler is the runtime.
ML compiler lowering decomposes into power-aware compilation — performance-correct code generation is the baseline; energy-optimal code generation under deadline constraints is the next level.
Power-aware compilation depends on accurate power/thermal models — the compiler can only optimize what it can predict. Temperature-dependent DVFS requires a thermal RC model of the chip.
RISC-V's vl register provides a compiler-controlled power knob with zero transition latency — a unique advantage over GPU/x86 frequency-based DVFS.
Compiler-directed power schedules feed into multi-tenant runtime scheduling — the compiler provides per-operator energy profiles that the runtime uses for power-capped scheduling decisions.
General scale-up strategy decomposes into chiplet-based scale-up — the physical mechanism for building systems larger than the reticle limit.
Chiplet scale-up depends on advanced packaging — CoWoS interposers are the physical substrate that connects chiplets.
Chiplet economics depend on process node selection — heterogeneous node mixing exploits the SRAM scaling gap.
UCIe D2D IP blocks are the digital IP that enables chiplet integration — the protocol layer bridges between on-chip and off-chip interconnects.
RISC-V chiplet thesis: different PE types (OoO for prefill, in-order for decode) on different chiplets, UCIe-connected, all RISC-V ISA.
Advanced packaging decomposes into 3D integration — the vertical stacking extension of 2.5D interposer-based packaging.
3D hybrid bonding enables chiplet stacking at much finer pitch than 2.5D — the physical enabler for heterogeneous 3D AI stacks.
3D stacking is thermally constrained — power must conduct through the stack. Thermal limits cap stacking at 2-3 active logic dies.
3D integration is a manufacturing response to physical limits — when transistors can't scale laterally, stacking vertically provides continued density improvement.
3D stacking enables heterogeneous node mixing — each die in the stack uses its optimal process node.
Tensor Cores decompose into the precision formats they consume — FP16, FP8, FP4 are the numerical representation that determines Tensor Core throughput and accuracy.
Precision choice directly shifts arithmetic intensity in the roofline model: half the bits per element doubles effective bandwidth for a given operation count.
HBM bandwidth growth lags compute growth — reducing precision is the primary lever for closing the bandwidth gap. FP4 halves memory traffic vs FP8.
RISC-V's VLA model enables software-controlled sub-byte blocking without silicon changes — BF16 support is ratified (Zvfbfwma), FP8 is proposed (Zvfofp8min).
FP4 inference reduces HBM capacity and bandwidth requirements, directly improving TCO by allowing more concurrent requests per GPU.
RISC-V matrix extension proposals target FP8/FP4 compute — the precision roadmap determines which matrix ISA is viable.
Digital IP blocks (DMA, NoC, memory controllers) decompose into analog/mixed-signal I/O PHYs — the physical layer that carries digital data off-die.
UCIe D2D PHYs are the physical enabler of chiplet architecture — without SerDes, chiplet disaggregation has no off-die communication path.
SerDes channel characteristics (loss, crosstalk) are determined by packaging — silicon interposer vs. organic substrate drives fundamentally different PHY architectures.
SerDes power (0.5-3 pJ/bit) is a significant fraction of total interconnect power budget — the D2D power wall constrains chiplet count and topology.
I/O chiplet node selection exploits the analog scaling wall — SerDes at N7 is ~30% cheaper than N3 with no performance penalty, enabling heterogeneous node mixing.
On-die NoC decomposes into off-die I/O — the SerDes is the bridge between intra-die NoC and inter-die D2D links.
Kernel-level mapping (GEMM, attention, element-wise) decomposes into multi-device parallelism — the same kernels run on each shard, coordinated by the parallelism strategy.
Parallelism strategy selection is constrained by the scale-up/scale-out boundary: TP within NVLink (scale-up), PP/DP across network (scale-out).
RISC-V clusters lack NVLink-equivalent intra-node bandwidth — favor FSDP + EP + PP over TP-heavy GPU configurations.
Training parallelism decomposes into inference parallelism — tensor parallelism for prefill, expert parallelism for decode, pipeline parallelism for disaggregated serving.
Within-model parallelism decomposes into across-model serving — multi-model scheduling builds on the sharding infrastructure provided by TP/PP/EP.
Every parallelism strategy depends on per-device runtime execution — the runtime manages the local computation and communication for each shard.
Distributed clusters decompose into the collective communication layer — AllReduce is the fundamental primitive that makes multi-node training convergent.
Every parallelism strategy depends on collectives: TP needs AllReduce inside layers, DP needs AllReduce for gradients, EP needs All-to-All for token routing.
Collective topology selection is constrained by the scale-up/scale-out boundary — ring within NVLink, hierarchical across InfiniBand.
On-die NoC decomposes into off-die collective communication — the same ring/tree topologies recur at different physical scales.
Distributed inference serving depends on collectives — prefill/decode disaggregation uses All-to-All for KV-cache redistribution.
GPU runtime (host/device split, streams, graphs) vs RISC-V runtime (unified ISA, no kernel launch overhead) — fundamentally different dispatch models for the same AI workload.
CUDA runtime instantiates the runtime layer in the DSL/compiler/runtime separation — the compiler produces PTX/SASS; the runtime dispatches it.
Efficient runtime dispatch via CUDA Graphs enables multi-model serving — graph capture and replay eliminate per-request launch overhead across heterogeneous models.
The per-tenant dispatch mechanism decomposes into the GPU runtime execution layer — tenant isolation depends on stream/graph partitioning.
The runtime dispatches the code the compiler produces — compiler lowering quality determines what the runtime has to work with.
RISC-V supply chain dynamics decompose into the broader AI chip bottlenecks — CoWoS, HBM, and node constraints affect RISC-V AI chips alongside GPU vendors.
CoWoS is the physical implementation of advanced packaging — capacity limitations in CoWoS directly constrain advanced packaging deployment for AI.
TSMC N3/N2 capacity allocation constrains which AI accelerators can use the most advanced nodes — node selection is not a free choice but a capacity-constrained one.
The CoWoS bottleneck explains why NVIDIA's market dominance persists — 60% allocation means competitors collectively can't match NVIDIA's volume.
Chip availability and HBM pricing are input assumptions in TCO models — a 15-20% HBM price increase directly raises accelerator BOM cost.
Inference-as-a-service business models depend on chip availability — token factory economics assume elastic GPU supply, which the CoWoS bottleneck disproves.
Semiconductor competitive landscape decomposes into the investment dynamics that fund it — capex decisions are bets on the cost deflation curve.
Token pricing deflation explains the inference-as-a-service business model — providers arbitrage the gap between infrastructure cost and token revenue.
The capex surge ($260B+) explains why supply chain bottlenecks persist — demand for CoWoS/HBM grows faster than capacity can expand.
Investment ROI depends on TCO models — the gap between per-token revenue and per-token infrastructure cost determines profitability.
FP4 and lower-precision formats are key hardware drivers of inference cost deflation — 2× throughput per generation directly reduces cost-per-token.
Parallelism strategies reduce inference latency and increase throughput, contributing to the cost deflation curve.
Beyond-CMOS physics decomposes into the interconnect scaling crisis — transistor improvement without wire improvement creates the physical bottleneck.
Wire RC scaling constrains process node migration — better transistors provide diminishing returns if wires don't improve.
Repeater insertion in digital IP blocks is fundamentally constrained by wire RC — the repeater wall at advanced nodes.
Wire RC contributes to interconnect power — the energy cost per bit-meter is set by the physical wire properties.
Advanced packaging (chiplets, 3D) is an architectural response to the wire delay problem — reducing wire distance between key components.
SerDes connects chiplets because global on-die wires are too slow — the chiplet boundary is defined by wire RC limits.
Chiplet architecture decomposes into inter-package NVLink domains — the physical chiplet connectivity scales up to rack-level via NVSwitch.
NVLink/NVSwitch is the canonical scale-up implementation — it creates a single large shared domain from multiple independent accelerators.
NCCL collective algorithms (Ring, Tree, PAT) are topology-optimized for NVSwitch — NVSwitch's non-blocking crossbar eliminates ring latency.
NVLink 5.0's 100 GB/s per lane depends on 112G PAM4 SerDes — the physical layer that enables the scale-up bandwidth.
The NVLink domain size determines the maximum tensor-parallel degree — NVL72 enables TP(72) without crossing into scale-out network.
NVLink is a proprietary GPU scale-up fabric; RISC-V clusters use open-standard scale-out networking — fundamentally different connectivity strategies.
SIMT execution model decomposes into the warp scheduler microarchitecture — the hardware mechanism that realizes the SIMT abstraction.
Warp scheduler dispatches MMA instructions to Tensor Cores — scheduler throughput determines Tensor Core utilization for AI workloads.
Occupancy is bounded by warp scheduler capacity — more resident warps than scheduler slots provides no benefit if warps can't be scheduled.
GPU hardware-managed warp scheduling vs RISC-V software-managed vector execution — two fundamentally different approaches to latency hiding.
The warp scheduler is a sub-component of the SM architecture described in the GPU overview.
